input: The Nusselt number is a dimensionless group that plays a central role in heat transfer at a surface, and it is typically introduced to second-year students when they first encounter convective transfer. In essence, the Nusselt number can be defined as the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer at a surface. The numerator of this ratio is the heat that is actually carried away from the surface by the moving fluid, while the denominator is the heat that conduction alone would carry across a stagnant layer of the same fluid, having the same thickness and subject to the same temperature difference. Since both terms are heat fluxes evaluated at the same surface, their ratio has no units, and the group essentially compares two mechanisms rather than measuring either one of them directly. A value near 1 means that the two terms are of the same size. At such a value, the moving fluid removes little more heat than a stagnant layer would conduct, and the surface transfer behaves much as conduction across the layer would behave. A large value, by contrast, means that the convective term is much the larger. The motion of the fluid then carries heat away far faster than conduction across the stagnant layer, and the surface transfer is governed by the flow rather than by the conductivity of the fluid alone. The group is formed from quantities that are held separately in a calculation: a heat transfer coefficient for the surface, a length that fixes the thickness of the comparison layer, and the thermal conductivity of the fluid. Read in that direction, the Nusselt number states how many times over the surface transfer exceeds pure conduction at the same scale. The group is widely used to report surface heat transfer in a form that can be compared across fluids, geometries, and flow rates, and to carry a measured or correlated coefficient from one size of equipment to another of the same shape. It is important to note that the comparison is local to the surface and to the chosen length. A value quoted without its length does not fix the transfer, because the conductive term in the denominator is set by that length.
